_note: Systems map of the fusion magnet supply chain (iteration 4). Built by tools/iter4_build.py from Sayari and public-source research. Stage 0 = mine ... 6 = fusion developer; policy nodes act on the chain.

lanes.label: Tape magnets (HTS: yttrium, nickel, copper, silver)

insights: The chains narrow to a few chokepoints: Chinese rare earth separators, Yunnan and Malaysian tin smelters, and a handful of tape and strand makers. Origin is lost at every one of them.
Harm sits at the left edge of the map, in mines run or taxed by armed groups (Kachin, Wa State, Rubaya), while fusion buyers sit at the right edge with no record linking the two ends.
The strongest evidence runs between companies (customs records, prospectuses, contracts). The weakest runs between mines and processors, which is exactly where the harm is.

Rules act unevenly: conflict-minerals laws cover tin and tungsten but not niobium or rare earths, sanctions hit named traders but not the plants that blend their ore, and public fusion funding carries no sourcing conditions at all.

Fusion has real leverage at one point: it buys most of the world's HTS tape, so tape makers can be asked to name their separators and target suppliers. Further upstream, fusion is too small to act alone.

hts_tape.text: Fusion is the main buyer of HTS tape. Faraday Factory's CEO told a 2025 industry Q&A that fusion consumes over 70% of current HTS production. About 15 makers exist worldwide; the top producers together exceed 3,000 km a year (12 mm width) and make more than half of global output. CFS's single 2026 order with Fujikura is over 10,000 km, about three times the leading producers' reported yearly output. So fusion buyers have real leverage over tape makers.

yttrium.text: World mine output was 10,000-15,000 t of yttrium oxide in 2025, mostly China with a significant share from Burma (USGS). Fusion's share is tiny. Our own estimate (not from a source; please check): a 2-micron YBCO layer on 4 mm tape holds about 7 g of yttrium per km, so 10,000 km of tape holds roughly 70 kg, around 0.001% of world supply. Many tapes use gadolinium or europium instead. Fusion has almost no market leverage over yttrium miners; its leverage is over tape makers, who can choose their oxide suppliers.

tin.text: World tin mine output was about 290,000 t in 2025; Myanmar 12,000 t, DRC 27,000 t (USGS). ITER's whole Nb3Sn order was 500 t of strand over 2008-2015, at most about 100 t a year, and strand is mostly copper. Even if it were all tin, that is under 0.04% of yearly tin output.

niobium.text: World niobium output was about 112,000 t in 2025, 93% from Brazil (USGS). ITER's peak strand output of about 100 t a year would be under 0.1% even if it were pure niobium.

tungsten.text: World tungsten output was about 85,000 t in 2025, 67,000 t from China (USGS). We found no public figure for the tonnage of tungsten in ITER's divertor, so fusion's share cannot be stated; it is certainly small next to cutting tools and alloys.

demand.argument: Fusion matters as a buyer only at the tape stage. For metals it is a rounding error, so pressure has to work through the handful of tape and strand makers, not through mines.

nodes.label: China October 2025 rare earth controls (extraterritorial rule), suspended for one year
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: Added a foreign-direct-product-style rule; suspended after the Trump-Xi deal. The April 2025 controls stayed in force, with general licences to selected exporters.

nodes.label: China export controls on tungsten items (Feb 2025)
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: USGS: China implemented export controls on selected tungsten items in February 2025; tungsten APT price roughly doubled in 2025.

nodes.label: US OFAC sanctions on the United Wa State Army (SDN 7825, since 2003)
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: Narcotics-related listing. The UWSA controls the Man Maw tin mine. Not a minerals sanction, but it makes direct dealings with UWSA entities illegal for US persons.

nodes.label: US Supplemental Burma Business Advisory (Jan 2024)
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: Warns that regime-linked militias, including Ministry of Defense border guard forces (OFAC-designated June 2023), are involved in rare earth extraction and that Burmese rare earths may be mislabelled as from other countries. Advisory only, not a ban.

nodes.label: US OFAC sanctions on PARECO-FF, CDMC, East Rise and Star Dragon (Aug 2025)
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: Treasury says CDMC sold minerals smuggled from PARECO-FF-controlled areas of Rubaya to Hong Kong exporters East Rise and Star Dragon.

nodes.label: Ukraine NSDC sanctions on Chepetsky Mechanical Plant (Oct 2022)
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: Ukraine lists the Rosatom strand maker; the US, EU and UK do not.

nodes.label: EU Conflict Minerals Regulation (3TG), in force for importers since 1 Jan 2021
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: Covers tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold as ores, concentrates and metals. Niobium is not covered. Applies only to EU importers up to the metal stage; companies 'beyond the metal stage' (strand, tape, magnet makers) have no obligations.

nodes.label: US Dodd-Frank s.1502 / SEC Form SD
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: SEC-reporting companies must disclose use of tin, tantalum, tungsten and gold from the DRC and adjoining countries. Niobium is not covered; neither is Myanmar. Private fusion firms such as CFS are not SEC reporters and do not file.

nodes.label: EU Critical Raw Materials Act (Reg. 2024/1252)
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: Lists heavy and light rare earths, niobium and tungsten as critical (tungsten also strategic); tin is not listed. Sets 2030 benchmarks: 10% extraction, 40% processing, 25% recycling, no more than 65% from one third country. A supply-security law; human rights appear only in strategic-partnership language.

nodes.label: EU CSDDD after Omnibus I (applies from 26 July 2029)
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: Narrowed to companies with over 5,000 employees and EUR1.5bn turnover. Fusion developers are start-ups far below these thresholds, so they fall outside it; only very large suppliers might be covered.

nodes.label: US DOE Milestone-Based Fusion Development Program
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: USD46m to eight firms in 2023 (CFS, Tokamak Energy's US arm, Type One, Realta, Focused, Princeton Stellarators, Xcimer, Zap). Payments tied to technical milestones. No sourcing or human-rights conditions were found in the award announcement.

nodes.label: Fusion Industry Association supply chain report (June 2026)
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: Tracks USD538m supply-chain spending in 2025. Its public summary does not mention critical minerals, human rights or conflict minerals.

nodes.label: RMI audits (RMAP) and ITSCI tagging
nodes.harmNote: Policy lever: Global Witness found all eight smelters sourcing Rwandan coltan passed RMI audits, at least four linked to likely Rubaya conflict coltan, and that smuggled ore was laundered with ITSCI tags. RMI disputes this. ITSCI has suspended or expelled six exporters since 2024.
